questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A baseline and the check that uses it
questions.learningObjective: State what a baseline records and how a check uses it
questions.stem: A translator's note flags a gap in the client's security annexe and asks what a baseline is for. Which reading is correct?

options.text: A recorded state of the configuration, used later as the reference point for comparison.
A checklist of improvements the client intends to deliver within the next financial year.
options.misconception: confuses a baseline with a roadmap of planned improvements

options.text: The minimum password and firewall settings that every system in the estate must share.
options.misconception: thinks a baseline is a set of common configuration values

options.text: A document that replaces the annual audit because it is generated automatically each week.
options.misconception: assumes a baseline replaces independent assurance

questions.explanation: A baseline is a snapshot of the agreed state, and a check compares the live estate against it to find drift. A plan of future improvements is not a reference point.
questions.hint: A baseline is a reference state, not a plan.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What separation of duties assumes
questions.learningObjective: Interpret approval counts as evidence about separated duties
questions.stem: While reviewing the client's annexe, a translator finds that 9 of 12 payment approvals were signed by one person and 3 by two. What does that pattern tell you about separation of duties?

options.text: The files were reviewed by an independent party, so the control is working as designed.
options.misconception: reads a review as evidence that approvals were separated

options.text: One person could both initiate and approve payments, which is what the control should prevent.
The three dual-signed approvals show the control is only partly effective in operation.
options.misconception: treats partial dual signing as a passing control outcome

options.text: Approval counts say nothing useful, because every genuine payment needs two sign-offs.
options.misconception: assumes two signatures are always required for a payment

questions.explanation: Separation of duties assumes the raiser is not the approver, so nine single-signed approvals show that assumption failing. A later review cannot restore a bypassed control.
questions.hint: Ask who could both raise and approve.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Choosing a cadence for a privileged access review
questions.learningObjective: Justify a review interval from the exposure it bounds
questions.stem: The glossary team asks why the client's privileged access review runs every quarter rather than every year. Write the explanation you would give.

answer.exemplar: A privileged account can change the shape of the estate in a single afternoon, and a quarterly cadence bounds how long an inappropriate right can survive undetected, while an annual cycle accepts twelve months of standing privilege before anyone checks. Cadence alone is not enough, but the interval must be short enough that the worst case is acceptable.

questions.explanation: The interval sets the worst case for undetected privilege, so an annual cycle accepts twelve months of standing access. The explanation must tie it to that exposure.
questions.hint: Tie the interval to the worst case.

options.text: The laptop return closed the leaver ticket correctly, so the gap is only a translation issue.
options.misconception: assumes the leaver process ended with the hardware

options.text: The account should stay open until the invoice is settled, since the work was completed.
options.misconception: thinks payment timing justifies keeping an account active

The project team should ask the contractor to stop using the account voluntarily.

questions.explanation: The leak appears because leaver handling closed against the device rather than the entitlements, so a right to shared data outlived the person. Revoking the right closes the gap.

questions.topic: What a retention requirement costs in storage
questions.learningObjective: Identify what drives the storage cost of a retention duty
questions.stem: During a terminology review, a translator is asked to compare retention cost and storage savings. Choose the pair, then the consequence.

options.text: Compressed backups and deduplication; together they remove the need for a retention schedule.
options.misconception: assumes storage tricks can replace a retention schedule

options.text: Archive tiers and cold storage; together they guarantee compliance without any review.
options.misconception: claims archive tiers deliver compliance without oversight

options.text: Legal holds and deletion logs; together they show which data must be kept.
options.misconception: picks legal mechanisms instead of the drivers of storage

options.text: The retention period and the record growth rate; together they size the storage a duty creates.

questions.explanation: A retention duty sizes storage by how much data accumulates in the period, so period and growth rate estimate the cost. Compression and tiers change where data sits, not how long data must be kept.
questions.hint: Cost follows the period and the volume.

options.misconception: pairs a contract with a control that belongs in engineering

questions.explanation: A privacy duty limits the data and reach a person has, so least privilege delivers it. Encryption supports a duty about data at rest, and a supplier contract is assurance.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A baseline and the check that uses it
questions.learningObjective: Separate what a baseline check proves from what it cannot
questions.stem: Before accepting the client's response, a translator writes a short note explaining what a check against a baseline can and cannot prove. Write the note.

answer.exemplar: A check compares the live estate with the recorded baseline and proves the difference between them, so it establishes whether the estate still matches what was agreed. It does not prove that the agreed state was the right one, that the baseline was complete, or that nothing changed and changed back between two runs.

questions.explanation: The check answers a narrow question about agreement and drift, so the note should keep evidence separate from proof. Overstating it makes the assurance look stronger than the baseline allows.
questions.hint: Separate agreement from adequacy.

questions.hint: Divide single approvers by all approvals.

options.misconception: assumes any fixed interval is too long regardless of context

options.misconception: concludes review frequency cannot matter for response

The problem is that the accounts were left in place, rather than that they were never reviewed.

options.misconception: treats a shared account as a handover convenience

options.misconception: thinks password rotation solves an attribution gap

questions.stem: The glossary entry for records retention covers two systems. System A stores 4 TB of records each year and must keep each year's records for 7 years. How much storage does system A hold under the duty at the end of year 7?

options.text: 7 TB, counting only the current year of records.
options.misconception: counts one year instead of the full retention span

options.text: 28 TB, from 4 TB a year held across the 7 years of the duty.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The engineering control behind a privacy obligation
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a duty needs a control as well as a policy
questions.stem: Somebody asks why a privacy obligation cannot be met by policy wording alone. Write the explanation you would give.

answer.exemplar: An obligation limits what may happen to a person's data, and a policy states an intention while a control makes the limit true in practice, so wording leaves the data reachable to whoever the system already permits. The engineering control is what makes the obligation enforceable, testable and consistent across every tool that touches the data.

questions.explanation: The distinction between intention and enforcement is the point, so the answer should show a control makes the duty verifiable. Policy alone can be satisfied on paper.
questions.hint: Policy states it; controls make it true.

options.misconception: invents a trend from a single pair of campaigns

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The joiner, mover and leaver gap that loses data
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a joiner, mover and leaver gap loses data
questions.stem: The notes explain how a joiner, mover and leaver gap loses data rather than merely causing delay. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: A gap loses data when access survives the person it belonged to, so the former employee's account can still read, copy or forward live records, and each such account is a channel that leaves no trace of who used it; with shared credentials the logs attribute the activity to the wrong person, and the discovery of the loss may come years later from a routine review rather than from any monitoring of the departure itself.

questions.explanation: The explanation should link surviving access to the loss itself, through shared credentials and absent attribution, rather than stopping at inconvenience.
questions.hint: Link surviving access to the data loss.

questions.stem: The glossary team asks a translator to explain how to choose a review cadence for privileged access. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The cadence should be set by the longest period in which an inappropriate right can sit unnoticed without causing unacceptable harm, so a team holding broad administrative rights over customer data needs a shorter interval than one holding a narrow reporting role; the decision should also record what happens when an owner does not respond, because a cadence with no fallback simply measures how often the same accounts are left in place.

questions.stem: A translator is asked to write the note explaining why a joiner, mover and leaver gap loses data rather than merely causing delay. Write it.

answer.exemplar: The gap loses data because the access that outlived the person still points at live records: a departed account can read, copy and forward, and with shared credentials the logs attribute that activity to whoever else used the same login, so the trail exists but names the wrong actor. questions.explanation: The note should link surviving access to the loss itself, through shared credentials and absent attribution, rather than stopping at inconvenience.

questions.topic: What an access recertification actually finds
questions.learningObjective: Choose the artefacts a completed recertification must leave
questions.stem: The annexe appendix lists what a recertification campaign must leave behind. Choose the pair, then the test.

options.text: The entitlement list and the owner list; the test is whether they are the same length.
options.misconception: compares list lengths rather than decisions

options.text: The ticket log and the closure dates; the test is whether the tickets were answered.
options.misconception: accepts a response as a decision

options.text: The campaign scope and the reviewer list; the test is whether both were approved.
options.misconception: confuses campaign paperwork with per-entitlement outcomes

options.text: The entitlements and the decision on each; the test is whether every one was decided.

questions.explanation: A campaign is complete only when every entitlement carries a decision, so what matters is the entitlements and the decision against each one. Lists describe the campaign, not outcomes.
questions.hint: The output is a decision, not a data set.
